title: Sudhana's pilgrimage
hook: a young seeker visits fifty-three teachers, among them a monk, a girl, a sailor and a king (Flower Garland, Gandavyuha)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Indra's net: a jewel at every knot, each one shining with all the others. Your line: each reflects all. Where did you see one person fill a whole room? Day one thousand one hundred ninety-four.

Who taught you the thing you actually live by? Not the answer you'd put on a form. The real one. Sometimes it turns out to be somebody nobody would have hired as a teacher: a grandmother, a coach, a bus driver, the kid at the next desk. A long section of the Flower Garland Sutra, called the Gandavyuha, is built on that surprise. A young man named Sudhana wants to learn how a bodhisattva lives, and instead of settling with one master, he sets off walking. Today: Sudhana's pilgrimage.
screen: `WHO TAUGHT YOU, REALLY?` → `NOT ALWAYS A TEACHER.` → `SUDHANA SETS OFF WALKING.`

segments.voice: It begins with Manjushri, the bodhisattva of wisdom. He meets Sudhana and sees how much he wants to learn. And he doesn't hand him the whole teaching. He tells him to go and find good friends, spiritual friends, and to ask each one how to follow the bodhisattva's way. Then he points him to the first. So Sudhana walks. And the teachers he finds are not who you'd expect. There's a monk, yes. But there's also a sailor who knows the sea and its dangers. There's a girl. There are laywomen and householders, a perfume seller, a boy, a king. Some are calm and gentle. A few are startling, and Sudhana has to wonder whether he's come to the right place. Tradition counts fifty-three of them. Here's the pattern that repeats, teacher after teacher. Sudhana arrives, bows, and asks. The teacher tells him what they know: one practice, one door into the way, opened as far as they've opened it. And then they say, more or less: this is the door I know. I can't tell you about the rest. Go on to the next. Teacher after teacher, however great, sends him further. Nobody keeps him. Nobody claims to have the whole of it. That changes the idea of wisdom. It isn't stored in one famous person on one mountain. It's spread out, a piece here, a piece there, in a harbor, in a palace, in a shop. Sudhana's whole job is to keep walking and keep asking, and to bow to whoever is standing in front of him. The next teacher might be the person about to be hurried past.
screen: `MANJUSHRI: GO FIND GOOD FRIENDS.` · `A MONK, A GIRL, A SAILOR, A KING.` · `EACH KNOWS ONE DOOR.` · `KEEP WALKING, KEEP ASKING.` · then, large: `FIFTY-THREE TEACHERS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: learn from someone unexpected. Settle, and let the breath slow down. Let a memory come of a time someone taught you something without meaning to. A stranger on a train. A remark from a coworker. A sentence overheard in a waiting room. Stay with that one moment. What door did they open that you hadn't found? Then let the memory go, and ask quietly who might be holding the next door: someone you'll pass today without a second look. Don't force an answer. Just keep the question open, the way Sudhana kept walking. The bell holds the time.
Sudhana's pilgrimage. A young seeker's long walk from teacher to teacher in the Flower Garland Sutra, each one knowing a single door. Today's word.
Your line: fifty-three teachers. Today, when someone unexpected says something useful, ask them one more question about it. Day one thousand one hundred ninety-four.

howItsDone: In East Asian Buddhism, Sudhana's journey is told as a model of seeking good spiritual friends, and his meetings with his teachers have been painted and carved in temples.

what it means: Sudhana learns from a monk, a sailor, a girl, a king and many more, each teaching one door and sending him on.
what a scholar hears: the Gandavyuha makes the good friend, kalyanamitra, the shape of the whole path; tradition counts fifty-three.

notes: All paraphrase. 'Tradition counts fifty-three' is kept because the index carry says fifty-three; counts vary by how teachers are tallied (Manjushri appears twice, etc.). Confirm wording.

Teachers named generically (monk, sailor/navigator, girl, laywomen, householders, perfume seller, boy, king). Confirm each type appears in the Gandavyuha (e.g., the navigator Vaira, King Anala, the perfume seller Utpalabhuti).
'A few are startling' alludes to teachers such as King Anala and Vasumitra; confirm the soft framing.
The repeated 'I know only this one door; go on to another' formula is paraphrased; confirm.
howItsDone mentions temple paintings and carvings; confirm or soften.
